title: The Pump and the Proof
topic: john snow and cholera in london
paragraphs: Cholera reached Britain for the first time in the autumn of 1831, at the port of Sunderland, and spread across the country over the following year.
It was terrifying in its speed: a healthy adult could be seized by violent diarrhea and vomiting in the morning and be dead of dehydration by nightfall.

The physicians of the day had an old explanation ready: miasma theory held that epidemic disease arose from foul air, the invisible emanations of rotting matter, stagnant drains, and overcrowded slums.
The theory matched experience, since the districts that smelled worst were usually those where the poor died fastest.
Edwin Chadwick, whose 1842 report launched Britain's public health movement, was a convinced miasmatist, and so was William Farr, the statistician of the General Register Office.
John Snow was an unlikely challenger.
Born in York in 1813, he had met cholera as a teenage apprentice treating miners at Killingworth colliery during that first epidemic.
By the late 1840s he was a London physician best known for anesthesia; in 1853 he would give chloroform to Queen Victoria at the birth of Prince Leopold.
If cholera were inhaled, he reasoned, it should first injure the lungs or poison the blood and announce itself with fever.
Instead it began in the gut.

The simplest explanation was that the agent had been swallowed, had multiplied in the intestine, and had left the body in the stools, ready to reach other mouths through soiled hands, soiled linen, and above all water.
Snow set out this case in 1849 in a short pamphlet, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, with examples of local outbreaks that a single contaminated supply seemed to explain.
He could not name the agent.

Filippo Pacini would describe a comma-shaped bacterium in cholera victims in Florence in 1854, in work that went almost unnoticed, and Robert Koch would not isolate the organism and convince the medical world until the 1880s.
Snow was proposing a living, self-reproducing poison on the strength of its behavior alone, and his critics did not find that persuasive.
At the end of August 1854, cholera erupted in Soho around Broad Street, and in roughly ten days more than five hundred people died within a few hundred yards of a single public pump.
Snow obtained the addresses of the dead from the General Register Office and walked the streets asking survivors where their households had drawn water.
The deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump, whose cool, clear water was popular.
On the evening of September 7 he put his findings to the parish Board of Guardians, and on the following day the pump's handle was removed.
What persuaded Snow was not only the cluster but the exceptions.
A workhouse near the pump, holding more than five hundred inmates, recorded only a handful of deaths; it had its own well.
A brewery on Broad Street employing about seventy men lost none of them; the workers drank the beer they made, and the brewery had its own well.
A widow in Hampstead, miles from Soho, died of cholera; she had liked the Broad Street water so much that a cart brought her a bottle of it each day.
Her niece, who visited and drank from the same supply, died as well.
People who shared Soho's air but not its water escaped; people who drank the water escaped nothing, however far away they lived.
Snow's most valuable local ally began as a doubter.
Henry Whitehead, a young curate in the parish, set out to disprove the water theory by his own door-to-door inquiry, and ended by confirming it.

He identified what now looks like the first case: an infant at 40 Broad Street who fell ill with diarrhea a few days before the outbreak, whose mother had rinsed the soiled napkins and emptied the water into a cesspool in front of the house.
A surveyor who opened the ground found the cesspool's brickwork decayed and the well of the pump only a few feet away.
The removal of the handle has become the founding legend of epidemiology, and like most legends it is tidier than the record.
Snow himself acknowledged that the outbreak was already subsiding when the handle came off, largely because so many residents had fled.
His celebrated map, with black bars marking the dead street by street, was drawn afterward as an instrument of persuasion rather than discovery; the theory came first.
None of this diminishes the work.
It means the pump was a demonstration, not the proof, and that the proof lay south of the river.
In south London two private companies, the Southwark and Vauxhall Company and the Lambeth Company, sold Thames water through pipes that ran down the same streets, often to houses side by side.

Both had once drawn from the river in the heart of the city, downstream of its sewer outfalls, but in 1852 the Lambeth Company moved its intake upstream to Thames Ditton, above the tidal reach and above the sewage; the Southwark and Vauxhall Company went on pumping from the tidal river at Battersea.

Hundreds of thousands of people, breathing the same air and often unaware of which company's pipe entered their house, had been divided without their knowledge into two groups that differed in one respect only.
No experiment could have been designed more cleanly, and this one had arranged itself on a grand scale.
The difficulty was practical: survivors in a stricken household frequently did not know which company served it.

Snow found a chemical answer: water from the tidal river carried far more salt, and a few drops of silver nitrate solution threw down a visibly heavier white precipitate of silver chloride when the sample came from the Southwark and Vauxhall Company.
With a bottle of the reagent and the addresses supplied by Farr's office, Snow traced the supply of house after house.

The figures he published in 1855 were stark: in the first seven weeks, cholera killed about 315 people for every ten thousand houses supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company, against 37 per ten thousand houses supplied by the Lambeth Company, and 59 in the rest of London.
A customer of the polluted supply was more than eight times as likely to die as a neighbor who drank from the clean one.
The reception was cool.
The General Board of Health's scientific committee, reporting in 1855, declined to accept Snow's conclusion and attributed the Soho outbreak to the state of the atmosphere.
When Snow told a parliamentary committee that same year that the city's offensive trades did not spread disease, The Lancet mocked him in an editorial.
The parish restored the pump handle once the outbreak had passed.
When Snow died of a stroke in 1858, at forty-five, the same journal's obituary ran to a few lines and praised his work on chloroform without mentioning cholera at all.
Vindication arrived by routes Snow did not live to see, some of them ironic.
Farr, who had long explained cholera's pattern by elevation and the cleaner air of higher ground, came to allow that the river water itself might be the link.
In 1866, when London's last cholera epidemic struck the East End, Farr traced it to a company that had supplied unfiltered water from the River Lea.

Meanwhile the hot summer of 1858 had produced the Great Stink, when the smell of the Thames drove members of Parliament from their chambers, and Parliament promptly funded Joseph Bazalgette's intercepting sewers to carry the city's waste downstream.
The sewers were built to abolish a smell.
In doing so they removed sewage from the stretch of river that the water companies drank from, and once they were complete cholera never returned to the capital.
It is tempting to tell this as one clear-eyed man against a blind establishment, and I think that framing does a disservice to both sides.
The miasmatists were wrong about the mechanism, but their drains and sewers saved lives, and Snow's opponents had a reasonable objection: he was asking them to believe in an organism no one had seen.
What Snow had, and what his critics lacked, was a method for deciding between explanations when the cause itself could not be observed.
Hold everything constant but the one suspected factor, count the dead on each side, and let the ratio speak.
That method, more than the pump handle, is his inheritance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, miasma theory attributed epidemic disease to
choices: contaminated drinking water drawn from the tidal Thames
a living organism that multiplied in the intestine
foul air given off by decaying matter and crowded slums
the violent diarrhea and vomiting that spread from the sick
the low elevation of the poorest districts above the river

proof.quote: miasma theory held that epidemic disease arose from foul air, the invisible emanations of rotting matter, stagnant drains, and overcrowded slums

questions.why: Paragraph 1 defines the theory directly: epidemic disease arose from foul air, the emanations of rotting matter, stagnant drains, and overcrowded slums.
distractorNotes: Reversed: contaminated water is Snow's explanation in paragraph 2, the rival of miasma theory.
Reversed: a living organism multiplying in the gut is Snow's proposal, not the miasmatists' view.
Outside the passage: the symptoms are described in paragraph 1, but nothing says the miasmatists blamed them for spreading disease.
Wrong paragraph: elevation is Farr's pattern in paragraph 11, and there too the explanation is cleaner air, not elevation itself.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Snow concluded that the cholera agent was swallowed rather than inhaled because
choices: the illness began in the gut, not with fever in the blood
the agent had been observed multiplying in the intestine
miners at Killingworth had all drunk from one contaminated well
the stools of victims were found to hold a living bacterium
fever and lung damage appeared only late in the course of the illness

proof.quote: it should first injure the lungs or poison the blood and announce itself with fever
Instead it began in the gut.

questions.why: Paragraph 2 lays out the reasoning: an inhaled poison should injure the lungs or blood and announce itself with fever, but instead cholera began in the gut, so the agent must have been swallowed.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 3 says Snow could not name the agent and argued from its behavior alone.
Outside the passage: Killingworth in paragraph 2 is where Snow first met cholera; no well is mentioned.
Wrong timing: paragraph 3 says the bacterium was not described until 1854, after Snow's 1849 argument.
Distortion: paragraph 2 says the illness began in the gut, not that fever and lung damage came later.

questions.stem: The author mentions Filippo Pacini and Robert Koch in paragraph 3 primarily to
choices: credit the scientists who first proved that Snow's theory was correct
show that the microscope had already made miasma theory untenable by 1849
argue that Snow deserves less credit than the men who found the organism
emphasize that Snow was arguing for an agent that no one had yet seen
explain why the Board of Health rejected Snow's conclusions in 1855

proof.quote: He could not name the agent.
Snow was proposing a living, self-reproducing poison on the strength of its behavior alone

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Snow could not name the agent, then dates the organism's discovery to 1854 and the 1880s, and concludes that he was proposing a living poison on the strength of its behavior alone. The two names mark how far ahead of the evidence he was working.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: paragraph 11 credits Farr and the sewers with vindication, and nothing says Koch proved Snow right.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the organism was not seen until 1854 and not accepted until the 1880s, well after 1849.
Outside the passage: the author never ranks Snow against Pacini or Koch.
Wrong paragraph: the Board of Health's rejection is in paragraph 10 and is tied to the atmosphere, not to Pacini or Koch.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the handle of the Broad Street pump was removed
choices: on the evening Snow addressed the Board of Guardians
the day after Snow presented his findings to the parish
roughly ten days after the first deaths, by Henry Whitehead
after a surveyor found the cesspool leaking into the well
once the General Register Office supplied the addresses

proof.quote: on the following day the pump's handle was removed

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says Snow put his findings to the parish Board of Guardians on the evening of September 7, and on the following day the handle was removed.
distractorNotes: Wrong timing: paragraph 4 says the handle came off the following day, not the same evening.
Wrong person: paragraph 6 introduces Whitehead as an investigator, not as the one who removed the handle.
Reversed order: the surveyor's inspection in paragraph 6 came after the handle was already off.
Half right: the addresses let Snow begin his inquiry, but the handle was removed only after he reported to the parish.

questions.stem: All of the following are cited in paragraph 5 as cases that persuaded Snow EXCEPT:
choices: a workhouse near the pump with its own well and few deaths
a brewery whose seventy workers drank beer and all survived
a widow in Hampstead who had the pump's water delivered
a niece who drank from the same supply and died
an infant whose soiled napkins went into a cesspool

proof.quote: it had its own well
lost none of them
a cart brought her a bottle of it each day
Her niece, who visited and drank from the same supply, died as well.
an infant at 40 Broad Street who fell ill with diarrhea a few days before the outbreak

questions.why: Paragraph 5 lists the workhouse, the brewery, the Hampstead widow, and her niece. The infant belongs to paragraph 6, where it is Henry Whitehead's finding, not one of Snow's exceptions.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5, sentence 2 gives the workhouse with its own well and only a handful of deaths.
Paragraph 5, sentence 3 gives the brewery that lost none of its seventy men.
Paragraph 5, sentence 4 gives the widow who had a bottle of the water brought by cart each day.
Paragraph 5, sentence 5 says the niece drank from the same supply and died as well.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the brewery workers on Broad Street escaped cholera because they
choices: did not drink the water that the public pump supplied
worked in air that was cleaner than the air of the street
had fled the neighborhood as soon as the outbreak began
lived outside Soho and came in only during the day
had survived an earlier attack and were immune

proof.quote: the workers drank the beer they made, and the brewery had its own well
People who shared Soho's air but not its water escaped

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the brewery workers drank the beer they made and the brewery had its own well, then sums up: people who shared Soho's air but not its water escaped. The workers were spared because they never drank from the pump.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 5 says the survivors shared Soho's air; it was the water they did not share.
Wrong paragraph: fleeing residents appear in paragraph 7, and nothing links them to the brewery.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about where the workers lived.
Outside the passage: the passage never mentions immunity from a previous attack.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Henry Whitehead
choices: was the physician who first proposed that cholera was waterborne
removed the handle from the Broad Street pump on Snow's advice
began his inquiry intending to refute the water theory
drew the map of deaths that Snow published in 1855
was the surveyor who found the decayed brickwork of the cesspool

proof.quote: set out to disprove the water theory by his own door-to-door inquiry, and ended by confirming it

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says Whitehead set out to disprove the water theory by his own door-to-door inquiry and ended by confirming it; he began as a doubter.
distractorNotes: Wrong person: paragraphs 2 and 3 give that role to Snow, and Whitehead was a curate, not a physician.
Wrong person: paragraph 4 says the parish removed the handle after Snow reported to the Board of Guardians.
Wrong person: paragraph 7 calls the map Snow's celebrated map.
Wrong person: paragraph 6 says a surveyor opened the ground; Whitehead identified the first case.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, the word 'instrument' most nearly means
choices: a device for taking measurements
a means of achieving a purpose
a formal legal document
a tool with a sharp edge
an object that produces music

proof.quote: as an instrument of persuasion rather than discovery

questions.why: Paragraph 7 calls the map an instrument of persuasion: something used to accomplish an end, in this case convincing others. The map was a means, not a measuring device or a musical object.
distractorNotes: A measuring device is a common meaning of the word, but the map measured nothing; it persuaded.
A legal instrument is another everyday meaning, and nothing in the sentence involves a document with legal force.
A cutting tool has nothing to do with a map of deaths.
The musical sense is the most familiar meaning, and it makes no sense applied to a map.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the popular story of the pump handle is best described as
choices: scornful and openly dismissive
uncritically admiring
entirely indifferent
admiring but corrective
bitterly disappointed

proof.quote: like most legends it is tidier than the record
None of this diminishes the work.

questions.why: Paragraph 7 calls the story a legend that is tidier than the record and sets the record straight, then adds that none of this diminishes the work. The author corrects the story while still admiring what Snow did.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author says plainly that none of this diminishes the work.
Reversed: the author spends paragraph 7 correcting the legend, which is the opposite of uncritical.
Too weak: the author cares enough to correct the record in detail.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 7 expresses disappointment; the correction is calm and measured.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in 1852 the Lambeth Company
choices: began selling filtered water drawn from the River Lea
laid new pipes in streets its rival did not serve
moved its intake downstream to Battersea, below the sewer outfalls
merged its supply with that of the Southwark and Vauxhall Company
shifted its intake upstream, above the tide and the sewage

proof.quote: the Lambeth Company moved its intake upstream to Thames Ditton, above the tidal reach and above the sewage

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says that in 1852 the Lambeth Company moved its intake upstream to Thames Ditton, above the tidal reach and above the sewage.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: the River Lea belongs to the 1866 East End epidemic in paragraph 11, and the Lambeth Company drew from the Thames.
Reversed: paragraph 8 says the two companies' pipes ran down the same streets.
Reversed: Battersea is where the Southwark and Vauxhall Company kept pumping; Lambeth moved upstream.
Outside the passage: the two companies are described as rivals serving neighboring houses, not as a merged supply.

questions.stem: The author notes in paragraph 8 that the two companies' pipes ran down the same streets primarily to
choices: criticize the wastefulness of competing private water companies
show that the two groups of customers differed in their water alone
explain why customers so often did not know which company served them
suggest that the two supplies were sometimes mixed in the pipes
contrast south London with the crowded streets of Soho

proof.quote: had been divided without their knowledge into two groups that differed in one respect only
No experiment could have been designed more cleanly

questions.why: Paragraph 8 builds to the point that the customers of the two companies breathed the same air and lived in the same streets, so they differed in one respect only: their water. The shared streets are what make the comparison clean.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the author never complains about waste or competition.
Answers a different question: customers' ignorance of their supplier is mentioned, but it is a side effect, not the reason the shared streets matter.
Outside the passage: nothing suggests the supplies mixed; the whole comparison depends on their staying separate.
Wrong purpose: paragraph 8 is not comparing neighborhoods; it is setting up a comparison between two water supplies.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Snow used silver nitrate to
choices: tell which company had supplied a house's water
measure how much sewage the tidal river carried
purify samples of water taken from the Broad Street pump
detect the cholera organism in the stools of victims
confirm that the Lambeth Company filtered its supply

proof.quote: a few drops of silver nitrate solution threw down a visibly heavier white precipitate of silver chloride when the sample came from the Southwark and Vauxhall Company

questions.why: Paragraph 9 explains that the saltier tidal water gave a heavier precipitate of silver chloride, which told Snow a sample came from the Southwark and Vauxhall Company when the household did not know.
distractorNotes: Half right: the test detected salt, not sewage, and it sorted samples by company rather than measuring pollution.
Wrong paragraph and wrong purpose: the Broad Street pump is in paragraphs 4 to 6, and the reagent sorted water, it did not purify it.
Contradicted: paragraph 3 says Snow could not name the agent, and the test was applied to water, not stools.
Outside the passage: filtering is never attributed to the Lambeth Company; the difference was where its intake sat.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, during the first seven weeks of the 1854 epidemic, a household supplied by the Lambeth Company was
choices: at greater risk than a household elsewhere in London
at no risk of cholera at all
as likely to lose a member as a household supplied by its rival
safer than the typical household in the rest of London
at risk only if it also drew water from a public pump

proof.quote: against 37 per ten thousand houses supplied by the Lambeth Company, and 59 in the rest of London

questions.why: Paragraph 9 gives 37 deaths per ten thousand Lambeth houses against 59 in the rest of London, so a Lambeth household did better than the London average, not just better than its rival's customers.
distractorNotes: Reversed: 37 per ten thousand is lower than the 59 for the rest of London, not higher.
Too extreme: 37 deaths per ten thousand houses is low, but it is not zero.
Contradicted: the rival's customers died at 315 per ten thousand, more than eight times the Lambeth rate.
Outside the passage: paragraph 9 says nothing about public pumps in south London.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following was part of the reception of Snow's work EXCEPT:
choices: A scientific committee attributed the Soho outbreak to the atmosphere.
A journal mocked him in an editorial.
Parliament ordered the pump sealed permanently.
The parish put the pump handle back after the outbreak.
His obituary praised his anesthesia work and omitted cholera.

proof.quote: attributed the Soho outbreak to the state of the atmosphere
The Lancet mocked him in an editorial
The parish restored the pump handle once the outbreak had passed.
praised his work on chloroform without mentioning cholera at all
The parish restored the pump handle

questions.why: Paragraph 10 gives the committee's verdict, the journal's mockery, the restored handle, and the obituary. Nothing says Parliament sealed the pump; the parish put the handle back.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 10, sentence 2 says the committee attributed the outbreak to the state of the atmosphere.
Paragraph 10, sentence 3 says The Lancet mocked him in an editorial.
Paragraph 10, sentence 4 says the parish restored the pump handle once the outbreak had passed.
Paragraph 10, sentence 5 says the obituary praised his chloroform work without mentioning cholera.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the sewers built after the Great Stink succeeded against cholera
choices: because Parliament had finally accepted Snow's theory
for a reason their builders had not set out to address at all
because the Lambeth Company had already moved its intake upstream
by filtering the water of the River Lea before it reached the East End
by driving the smell of the river away from the Houses of Parliament

proof.quote: The sewers were built to abolish a smell.
they removed sewage from the stretch of river that the water companies drank from

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says the sewers were built to abolish a smell, and that in doing so they removed sewage from the river the water companies drank from. The builders aimed at the air; the benefit came through the water.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 11 says the sewers were built to abolish a smell, which is miasma reasoning, not Snow's.
Wrong link: the Lambeth move in paragraph 8 concerned one company's intake, not the sewers.
Wrong paragraph: the River Lea is tied to the 1866 East End epidemic and to Farr, not to Bazalgette's sewers.
Half right: driving away the smell was the goal, but the passage credits the result to removing sewage from the water supply.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the method the passage credits to Snow in paragraph 12?
choices: A chemist isolates a bacterium from a sample of river water and grows it in culture
A city builds new sewers after a hot summer makes the river's smell unbearable
A physician notes that patients with a fever recover faster in rooms with open windows
An inspector condemns a well because its brickwork is cracked and a cesspool lies nearby
A farmer sows two fields with the same seed, waters only one, and compares the yields

proof.quote: Hold everything constant but the one suspected factor, count the dead on each side, and let the ratio speak.
two groups that differed in one respect only

questions.why: Paragraph 12 states the method: hold everything constant but the one suspected factor, count the outcome on each side, and let the ratio speak. Two fields alike in everything but watering, with the yields compared, is that method in a new setting.
distractorNotes: Wrong method: isolating the organism is what Koch did in paragraph 3, and it is exactly what Snow could not do.
Wrong method: that is the Great Stink response from paragraph 11, action without a comparison.
Wrong method: nothing is held constant; the physician is noticing a pattern, not controlling for other differences.
Wrong method: that is the surveyor's inspection from paragraph 6, a finding about one site rather than a comparison between groups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: The removal of the Broad Street pump handle ended cholera in London and proved that miasma theory was false
Victorian physicians rejected Snow's theory because they were unwilling to abandon the sanitary reforms it threatened
Koch's isolation of the cholera bacterium finally gave Snow's followers the proof he had lacked
Snow's lasting contribution was a method for testing an unseen cause by comparison, not the famous pump
The miasma theory was harmless in practice because the sewers it inspired happened to remove cholera's true source

proof.quote: the pump was a demonstration, not the proof, and that the proof lay south of the river
What Snow had, and what his critics lacked, was a method for deciding between explanations when the cause itself could not be observed.
That method, more than the pump handle, is his inheritance.

questions.why: The passage sets up miasma theory, tells the pump story and then deflates it as a demonstration rather than the proof, walks through the south London comparison, and closes by naming the comparative method as Snow's inheritance. Only the answer captures that arc.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 7 says the outbreak was already subsiding when the handle came off, and paragraph 11 says cholera returned in 1866.
Outside the passage: the author never gives that motive; paragraph 12 says the critics' objection was the unseen organism.
Outside the passage: Koch appears only in paragraph 3, and paragraph 11 credits vindication to Farr and the sewers.
Too strong and one detail only: paragraph 12 calls the miasmatists wrong about the mechanism, and the sewers are one irony in paragraph 11, not the thesis.
